chapter: Early bands around Bay St. Louis
title: Advertising trucks and the Cigar Stomp
summary: Bands advertised dances from trucks; George McCollum improvised a tune nobody knew and it was named the Cigar Stomp, around 1928.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Yeah. How did that work? I never heard about this.

We'd come over here to play a dance and we'd make an advertisement on the truck just like we used to advertise in the Orleans. And I'll never forget George McCollum pick up a number and nobody would know what he was playing. And he didn't know it either, but it sounded something good. And everybody just followed him in it, you know. He followed him and went on to play it, took chorus and everything. It sounded good. So after we finished, I asked George, I said, what's the name of that number? George said, well the man will give us a cigar every time we play. He said, let's call it the cigar stomp. Do you remember that? Sure I remember that. I remember that as good as it goes. Right out there by that drugstore. That's about the last part of 28, the first part of 29, before we left on the tour. That was about 28.
McCollum just made it up like that, huh? Oh yeah.

He went to pick up another number and... It must have slipped his mind. So the key for making the band sound right, just went on playing his horn, stayed in the key, you see. And he played something and it sounded good. So he called it the cigar stomp.
And the chords just fitted in? It was good.

We followed him. We followed him. Every time he'd make a note, we knew the chord changes. She'd had a good drummer, good bass, good banjo player. And when he started to numb in the keyboard, you know, right with him. Or you can follow him at that time. Yeah.
